items.originalTitle: Data Processing Incidents on Inference Providers
items.summary:
OpenRouter disclosed that security researchers identified data processing incidents involving several inference providers, prompting OpenRouter to off-board three providers and remove 125 endpoints from its Zero Data Retention (ZDR) program. The company confirmed no breach or unauthorized access occurred on its own platform and has notified all potentially affected customers.

OpenRouter is collaborating with researchers and providers to investigate the findings and is implementing ongoing testing and network path verification to prevent future incidents. The company requires validation before restoring ZDR eligibility to any affected endpoints and is encouraging providers to publish incident reports. Notable affected providers include Novita, Phala, and Together, each having issued security notices related to these incidents.

Anil Seth, a neuroscience professor and consciousness researcher, challenges the idea that artificial intelligence can be truly conscious, suggesting consciousness is tied to biological life rather than computation. He highlights cultural and ethical concerns surrounding the pursuit of conscious AI, noting that many fictional and real-world examples show potential risks and misunderstandings about machine consciousness.

Seth discusses the psychological reasons people conflate intelligence with consciousness and emphasizes the moral implications if AI systems were to become conscious or appear conscious. He warns that misattributing consciousness to AI could distort ethical priorities and human self-understanding, urging caution in how society approaches the development and treatment of AI technologies.

items.originalTitle: Together.ai: Prompt Leakage for Requests
items.summary:
Together AI reported a security incident where an unauthorized party accessed stored prompt samples from its serverless inference service after a credential for a private repository was exposed in a public GitHub repository. The exposure occurred during June and July 2026, affecting prompts submitted to several AI models, and the company is investigating the scope and impact on customer data.

The incident involved an AI coding agent accidentally committing a credential that granted access to a private Hugging Face repository containing prompt samples. Together AI detected and reverted the exposure but confirmed that an unauthorized party downloaded the data and tested some credentials found within. The company has engaged forensic investigators and law enforcement, strengthened security controls, and is reviewing affected data to notify impacted customers as needed.

items.title: Researchers disclose Upload2Shell vulnerability in Ghostscript's font loader affecting Google, WordPress, Debian 13, Zoom, Box, and others
items.originalTitle: One Vulnearbility Hacks Google, WordPress, Roundcube, Debian 13, Zoom, Box, etc.
items.summary:
Researchers have identified a use-after-free vulnerability named Upload2Shell (CVE-2026-125396) in Ghostscript's Type 1 font loader that enables remote command execution by bypassing its -dSAFER sandbox. This flaw affects multiple widely used platforms and applications, including Google services, WordPress, Roundcube, Debian 13, Zoom, and Box, through common file upload and image processing features that invoke Ghostscript indirectly.

The vulnerability arises when trusted file extensions like .jpg or .png are passed to Ghostscript via image processing libraries such as ImageMagick, which delegates rendering to Ghostscript. Attackers can craft malicious documents that exploit this flaw to execute arbitrary commands on affected systems. The researchers reported the issue to Artifex and collaborated with impacted platforms to mitigate the risk, though some fixes are still in progress.

This discovery highlights the risks of complex file processing dependencies and the challenges of securing interpreters embedded within popular software. Users and administrators are advised to apply updates promptly once patches become available to reduce exposure to this critical security issue.

items.summary:

The firm highlights recent disruptions, including Microsoft outages and financial sector phishing campaigns, as indicators of a growing cyber epidemic fueled by AI capabilities.

The report notes that while defensive programs have uncovered vulnerabilities at unprecedented rates, attackers only need to find one exploit, and zero-day vulnerabilities have doubled since the release of cyber-capable open-source AI models. Policy responses in countries like Japan and South Korea are emerging but remain insufficient, especially given the reliance on open-source software maintained by under-resourced volunteers. The expanding attack surface, driven by AI-generated code, further accelerates the cyber arms race, suggesting that without coordinated and forceful policy action, cyber warfare risks will continue to escalate.

The study uncovered evidence of compromises at three AI providers, unauthorized prompt access by inference marketplace resellers, and widespread failures to honor privacy settings and data retention policies.

The research highlighted risks in AI inference data handling, including prompt data being transmitted across multiple organizations and marketplaces, sometimes ending up in unexpected locations such as internal company chats in China. The findings emphasize the need for stronger security measures and transparency in AI supply chains to protect sensitive customer data and maintain privacy.

Muru

Graham Dumpleton started mod_wsgi 20 years ago, and has been thinking about the ideal way to serve Python web applications in production ever since.

Muru is his new, AI-assisted Rust server that aims to provide the best possible tools for running ASGI and WSGI Python apps both in development and production.

As he did with wrapture, he's been publishing an extraordinarily detailed account of the project as he works on it - as part of his development process.

Here's everything he's published so far, all in the last three weeks:

  • 2026-11-04 — Twenty years of mod_wsgi, and what comes next
  • 2026-11-05 — A first look at Muru
  • 2026-11-07 — Muru: looking inside the workers
  • 2026-11-08 — Muru: how it fits together
  • 2026-11-09 — Muru: import once, fork many
  • 2026-11-10 — Muru: HTTPS in development
  • 2026-11-11 — Muru: WSGI and ASGI together
  • 2026-11-11 — AI as a lifestyle choice
  • 2026-11-12 — Muru: releases, not restarts
  • 2026-11-13 — Muru: canaries without a service mesh
  • 2026-11-14 — Muru: a better tenant in a container
  • 2026-11-15 — Muru: working with Kubernetes, not around it
  • 2026-11-16 — Muru: scaling from what the workers report
  • 2026-11-17 — Muru: scaling to zero

  • 2026-11-21 — Muru: tracing in the toolbar

That post about AI as a lifestyle choice is particularly worth a read:

The AI may be doing a lot of the work on the surface, but deciding what isn't good enough yet is still down to me, and twenty years of getting things wrong with mod_wsgi turns out to be useful for that. I am prepared to put in the hard work to keep polishing Muru until it is something I would trust, and something you would too.

items.title: Can Jensen Really Return?
items.originalTitle: Can Jensen Really Return?
items.summary:
Welcome, Weekenders! 

Jensen Huang wants a mulligan, and a good number of people seem keen to let him have one.

On Tuesday, just days after the longtime Nvidia CEO resigned the job, Huang said in a statement he’d be open to taking back the job. Depending on your perspective, that suggestion is akin to letting a skunked dog back into bed—or a veritable Second Coming. For now, Nvidia’s board is holding firm and has continued to insist it won’t rehire Huang. 

One of the most prominent calls for Huang’s return came on Friday, with President Donald Trump saying he thought Nvidia should give Huang his job back. “We’re a country of second chances,” Trump said. “He’s a man ... who made some bad decisions.” (Surely a situation Trump himself could understand.) 

In addition to Trump, a good number of industry pooh-bahs have continued to voice support for their fallen comrade and advocating for Huang was definitely a major topic on this week’s very busy conference circuit. 

That support came in both implicit and explicit terms. At the New York Times’ DealBook Summit, Elon Musk was blunt, saying “there’s no one who can really replace” Huang. At the TomorrowX conference, former Uber CEO Travis Kalanick and Musk groupie Antonio Gracias donned black leather jackets to show their solidarity. And during a Semafor shindig in San Francisco, Sam Altman described Huang as a personal hero, Jeff Bezos said he was a “remarkable guy” and investor Bill Ackman labeled him as “one of the most iconic CEOs of all time.” 

On X, Ackman has been theorizing about how Huang could actually return. Ackman (and venture capitalist Garry Tan) has been trumpeting a roundabout plan that involves getting together a 15% ownership block of Nvidia to call a special shareholder meeting and then ... vote out the anti-Huang board members ... and swing the board to a pro-Huang majority? It’s somewhat unclear. (Apparently, Huang still has some allies on the board; remember, we told you that the board hadn’t initially wanted to act at all.)

“Ackman’s idea is somewhere between extremely unlikely and remote,” said Jeffrey Gordon, a Columbia University law professor and former Treasury Department attorney. (Or, in other words, as likely as defrosting a 20-pound Thanksgiving turkey overnight.) The proposal does seem to assume Huang supporters could really rile up Wall Street institutions with major Nvidia stakes, such as BlackRock, and get them to go activist—not a certain thing at all. It also conveniently ignores how difficult the math for a board-ousting vote looks when factoring in how much institutional money is held in passive-investing funds, which will never throw support behind an insurrection. 

Rather than a board coup, Huang’s clearest route to returning would be if the board caves and changes its mind. Sure, it might, eventually. But we have to get through the many, many inquiries into Huang and Nvidia that have popped up and who knows what else we’ll learn in the meantime, especially since there are a lotttt of people newly determined to peer into every Nvidia crevice: journalists galore, the SEC, the Commerce and Justice Departments, a trio of Congressional committees and possibly the FBI.

The Huang situation keeps getting likened to Altman’s ouster from OpenAI in 2023, which obviously ended with Altman’s return. I don’t think the comparison holds up. Most obviously, OpenAI was a private company—its board had more freedom to change its mind. And as Gordon pointed out to me, Altman’s reinstatement came after a true mass rebellion of OpenAI staff: roughly 745 out of 770 employees signed a letter threatening to go with Altman to Microsoft, more than 95% of the company. Now, a letter supporting Huang’s reinstatement is floating around the internet, and it purports to have signatures from 10,263 Nvidia employees. Even if they were all legit signatures, they represent only a quarter of the company’s workforce.Maybe most Nvidians, as they call themselves, actually didn’t like Huang’s rampant humiliation tactics, which reportedly once included a threat to scalp someone and piss on their brain. Maybe most of them are comfortable living without him. I mean, sure, I’d totally get why!—Abram Brown (abe@theinformation.com)

Listening: “Stories of Art”

After weeks like the ones we’ve just had, I like to make it a point to visit a museum and spend some time staring at ancient, beautiful things—a chance to relish the creative ingenuity of humans who never once heard the phrase “forward-deployed engineer.”

Truthfully, though, the tech action has lately been so fast-paced that I still haven’t gotten to make one of those pilgrimages, so I’ve been counterprogramming my brain with a binge through “Stories of Art,” a podcast about, yes, art—from Renaissance Florence to Basquiat’s lower Manhattan loft—that launched earlier in the year. (Apple recently declared it one of 2026’s best.) The hosts are a pair of amiable Brits, art historian James Fox and art critic Alastair Sooke, who take a cheerful, conversational approach to what might otherwise be dry recountings. In effect, they are to Renoir what “The Rest Is History” lads are to the Romans. (Given the subject matter of “Stories of Art”—namely, art—I suggest you watch the podcast’s video version when you can. While Fox and Sooke are quite adept at describing the artworks they mention, it’s nice to actually see what they’re talking about.) 

Nearly all the artists who get mentioned achieved their fame through real entrepreneurial verve, challenging the entrenched status quo. (Sounds like a familiar motivation, right?) Take Claude Monet and the birth of Impressionism: The movement traces its origins to a decision in 1874 by Monet and a group of other artists to refuse to exhibit their work at an established gallery. Instead, they formed their own company (yes, founder mode Monet!) and then set up their own Paris exhibition space that featured newfangled technology, such as elevators. Many of you will enjoy one of the most recent episodes on James Whistler, a fellow who took a real dim view of journalists and pursued a high-profile libel lawsuit against one critic. A warning about how that turned out for Whistler: He did triumph in court. He then promptly went bankrupt.—Abram Brown 

Reading: “Fruit Fly” by Josh Silver

In suburban north London, author Mallory Maddox seems to have a rich, full life: a handsome Netflix-executive husband, a townhome with $2,000 armchairs and dusky-pink walls and a literary world standing as a “modern-day Virginia Woolf,” as one reviewer has christened her. Yet appearances are almost always deceiving in “Fruit Fly,” a spry, tart satire of sex and 21st century storytelling: Mallory’s relationship with hubbie Ronan has turned stiff and chilly, and as much as he thinks about the bedroom, it’s to insist that it’s time for kids. (“I haven’t had an orgasm in years,” she recalls in an ongoing inner monologue.) Professionally, Mallory is dogged by “a shadowy, persisting darkness”—a profound case of writer’s block. To fill the time, she moonlights as an online therapist and hunts exhaustively for those expensive home furnishings.

Desperate for writerly inspiration, she peruses Reddit—uh oh—and takes to heart another author’s comment about the state of the publishing industry: “go dark, go gay.” She downloads Grindr, sets up an account with a few of her husband’s nudes and scores an invite to an orgy at a house down the street. She never actually sets foot inside but nevertheless makes the acquaintance of Leo, an attractive but homeless and drug-addicted gay man who sells himself to other men. (As the novel shifts perspectives, Leo contributes his own inner thoughts, which are often mordant and felonious. “Old women carry cash. Everyone knows that,” he thinks, snatching a purse. “Someone should tell them to stop.”) Mallory offers to counsel Leo—pro bono, bless her—and begins writing a novel that lightly fictionalizes his frayed life. For a time, he believes she’s just a daffy do-gooder. (“This is weird,” Leo thinks as she leads him through a silent-breathing exercise. “This is very fucking weird, but I guess I’ve done weirder things.”) And her publishers absolutely adore what she is finally putting on the page. As one editor remarks: “It’s so bleak—but also somehow so funny?” Much the same can be said about “Fruit Fly” itself.—A.B.

Watching: “The Weight”

President Franklin Roosevelt attempted to govern Depression-era America through no small number of novel schemes: A good many of them are quite famous, such as Social Security. A few have disappeared into history, including Roosevelt’s 1933 executive order that banned gold hoarding, forcing Americans to turn over large stockpiles of the precious metal. (No one could keep more than $100 worth.) That presidential decision is the inciting force in “The Weight,” a tense wilderness thriller starring Ethan Hawke as Murphy, leader of a group of convicts hired by their jailer (Russell Crowe) to heist a gold mine’s reserves. It’s part of a plan that’s complex in the same way that “Goldfinger” is not actually a film about robbing Fort Knox. 

Often, heist films are fabulous capers, with champagne, tuxedos and bon mots. “The Weight” very much is not, depicting a bloodied-knuckled trek across the Oregon backwoods, with Murphy and his thieves weighed down, literally, by their bullion-filled backpacks and, metaphorically, by their past misdeeds and inner demons. Still, Murphy is well incentivized to make it through. In a true miscarriage of justice, he has been separated from his plucky daughter, Penny (Avy Berry); part of his reward for orchestrating the robbery is early release, which will let him reclaim her. “The Weight” does take a moment to get going. Then it really rips, with a pair of memorable fight scenes that are a real credit to both the film’s editing and cinematography.—A.B.

Now, a letter supporting Huang’s reinstatement is floating around the internet, and it purports to have signatures from 10,263 Nvidia employees. Even if they were all legit signatures, they represent only a quarter of the company’s workforce.Maybe most Nvidians, as they call themselves, actually didn’t like Huang’s rampant humiliation tactics, which reportedly once included a threat to scalp someone and piss on their brain. Maybe most of them are comfortable living without him. I mean, sure, I’d totally get why!—Abram Brown (abe@theinformation.com)

Listening: “Stories of Art”

After weeks like the ones we’ve just had, I like to make it a point to visit a museum and spend some time staring at ancient, beautiful things—a chance to relish the creative ingenuity of humans who never once heard the phrase “forward-deployed engineer.”

Truthfully, though, the tech action has lately been so fast-paced that I still haven’t gotten to make one of those pilgrimages, so I’ve been counterprogramming my brain with a binge through “Stories of Art,” a podcast about, yes, art—from Renaissance Florence to Basquiat’s lower Manhattan loft—that launched earlier in the year. (Apple recently declared it one of 2026’s best.) The hosts are a pair of amiable Brits, art historian James Fox and art critic Alastair Sooke, who take a cheerful, conversational approach to what might otherwise be dry recountings. In effect, they are to Renoir what “The Rest Is History” lads are to the Romans. (Given the subject matter of “Stories of Art”—namely, art—I suggest you watch the podcast’s video version when you can. While Fox and Sooke are quite adept at describing the artworks they mention, it’s nice to actually see what they’re talking about.) 

Nearly all the artists who get mentioned achieved their fame through real entrepreneurial verve, challenging the entrenched status quo. (Sounds like a familiar motivation, right?) Take Claude Monet and the birth of Impressionism: The movement traces its origins to a decision in 1874 by Monet and a group of other artists to refuse to exhibit their work at an established gallery. Instead, they formed their own company (yes, founder mode Monet!) and then set up their own Paris exhibition space that featured newfangled technology, such as elevators. Many of you will enjoy one of the most recent episodes on James Whistler, a fellow who took a real dim view of journalists and pursued a high-profile libel lawsuit against one critic. A warning about how that turned out for Whistler: He did triumph in court. He then promptly went bankrupt.—Abram Brown 

Reading: “Fruit Fly” by Josh Silver

In suburban north London, author Mallory Maddox seems to have a rich, full life: a handsome Netflix-executive husband, a townhome with $2,000 armchairs and dusky-pink walls and a literary world standing as a “modern-day Virginia Woolf,” as one reviewer has christened her. Yet appearances are almost always deceiving in “Fruit Fly,” a spry, tart satire of sex and 21st century storytelling: Mallory’s relationship with hubbie Ronan has turned stiff and chilly, and as much as he thinks about the bedroom, it’s to insist that it’s time for kids. (“I haven’t had an orgasm in years,” she recalls in an ongoing inner monologue.) Professionally, Mallory is dogged by “a shadowy, persisting darkness”—a profound case of writer’s block. To fill the time, she moonlights as an online therapist and hunts exhaustively for those expensive home furnishings.

Desperate for writerly inspiration, she peruses Reddit—uh oh—and takes to heart another author’s comment about the state of the publishing industry: “go dark, go gay.” She downloads Grindr, sets up an account with a few of her husband’s nudes and scores an invite to an orgy at a house down the street. She never actually sets foot inside but nevertheless makes the acquaintance of Leo, an attractive but homeless and drug-addicted gay man who sells himself to other men. (As the novel shifts perspectives, Leo contributes his own inner thoughts, which are often mordant and felonious. “Old women carry cash. Everyone knows that,” he thinks, snatching a purse. “Someone should tell them to stop.”) Mallory offers to counsel Leo—pro bono, bless her—and begins writing a novel that lightly fictionalizes his frayed life. For a time, he believes she’s just a daffy do-gooder. (“This is weird,” Leo thinks as she leads him through a silent-breathing exercise. “This is very fucking weird, but I guess I’ve done weirder things.”) And her publishers absolutely adore what she is finally putting on the page. As one editor remarks: “It’s so bleak—but also somehow so funny?” Much the same can be said about “Fruit Fly” itself.—A.B.

Watching: “The Weight”

President Franklin Roosevelt attempted to govern Depression-era America through no small number of novel schemes: A good many of them are quite famous, such as Social Security. A few have disappeared into history, including Roosevelt’s 1933 executive order that banned gold hoarding, forcing Americans to turn over large stockpiles of the precious metal. (No one could keep more than $100 worth.) That presidential decision is the inciting force in “The Weight,” a tense wilderness thriller starring Ethan Hawke as Murphy, leader of a group of convicts hired by their jailer (Russell Crowe) to heist a gold mine’s reserves. It’s part of a plan that’s complex in the same way that “Goldfinger” is not actually a film about robbing Fort Knox. 

Often, heist films are fabulous capers, with champagne, tuxedos and bon mots. “The Weight” very much is not, depicting a bloodied-knuckled trek across the Oregon backwoods, with Murphy and his thieves weighed down, literally, by their bullion-filled backpacks and, metaphorically, by their past misdeeds and inner demons. Still, Murphy is well incentivized to make it through. In a true miscarriage of justice, he has been separated from his plucky daughter, Penny (Avy Berry); part of his reward for orchestrating the robbery is early release, which will let him reclaim her. “The Weight” does take a moment to get going. Then it really rips, with a pair of memorable fight scenes that are a real credit to both the film’s editing and cinematography.—A.B.

Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line. No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.

items.summary:
On a sunny day in San Francisco last month, Anthropic Chief Financial Officer Krishna Rao and other executives huddled in the company’s downtown headquarters to brief major investors on its latest financials—and assuage concerns.

Revenue growth in the third quarter had fallen from its torrid pace. Privately, some investors doubted that the company could go public at the $1.5 trillion valuation bandied about for months, especially as AI-related stocks took a beating.

Throughout the month, Rao and his squad countered those concerns by highlighting growth opportunities in fields from life sciences to chip design, say people familiar with the conversations.

As for the broader market’s jitters? Ignore it, they told investors. That turned out to be decent advice: By Thursday’s close, Anthropic was worth $1.76 trillion on a fully diluted basis.

items.originalTitle: Anthropic’s IPO Triumph
items.summary:
Anthropic pulled it off. The biggest pure-play AI company out there, maker of the Claude line of AI models, went public on Thursday, with its shares jumping as much as 39% above its IPO price. The stock settled back a bit to close at $97.17, up 17% from its IPO price. That gave it a market capitalization of $1.76 trillion, assuming you include all options, restricted stock units and convertible notes that might one day become shares. Not bad for a company that’s just five years old.

What makes the IPO even more notable is that it occurred despite months of investor jitters about the cost of AI development. Partly as a result of those jitters, we’ve had a very choppy market that has stalled IPO plans by a slew of other companies—including data center developers SB Energy and Nscale that filed publicly over the summer. Notably, SB Energy on Thursday updated its IPO filing for the first time since late September, suggesting it was still hoping to go public, while Nscale updated its filing a week ago also for the first time since September. But Anthropic’s success doesn’t mean the IPO market has opened up. “I don't think this opens the floodgates unless you look like Anthropic,” Lise Buyer, managing partner of Class V Group, said on a subscriber video discussion convened by The Information.
